name: Tumescent liposuction
lead: Tumescent liposuction is a liposuction technique in which large volumes of dilute lidocaine and epinephrine are infiltrated into subcutaneous fat before fat is aspirated through thin cannulas. The solution numbs the area and constricts blood vessels to reduce bleeding, so the procedure can be done under local anesthesia.[1][2][21] It is credited to dermatologic surgeons Jeffrey Klein and Patrick Lillis, who developed it in the 1980s; it was marketed in the 1990s.[1][21]

For appearance, it is used to remove localised fat deposits that persist despite diet and exercise, sculpting the contour of areas such as the abdomen, flanks, thighs, arms, chin and neck. The American Society of Plastic Surgeons describes liposuction as contouring for people of normal weight with some extra fat and firm, elastic skin, not as a treatment for obesity or cellulite.[1][24] People who choose it describe a slimmer, more defined silhouette, and cosmetic surgeons also use it for high-definition body contouring around muscle outlines.[1]

Because fat cells that are removed do not return to that spot, results in the treated area are lasting, although studies cited by Wikipedia report that overall body fat tends to return to its earlier level within months if lifestyle is unchanged, with some of it redistributing to untreated areas.[1][21]

It is a standard approach to body contouring and is also used for lipedema. Safety data come largely from surveys of dermatologic surgeons; a 1999 analysis of deaths and surveys of tens of thousands of procedures have been published, and the main specific concern discussed in the literature is lidocaine dosing.[3][4][5][6]

paras: The tumescent method swells the target fat with infiltrated fluid until it is firm. The fluid contains lidocaine for anesthesia and epinephrine to limit bleeding, allowing patients to remain awake, according to the literature on the technique.[2][3] Wikipedia notes that American dermatologists developed local-anesthetic-only methods in the 1980s, leading to the tumescent technique, and that the approach removes the need for sedatives or narcotics during the procedure.[1]

Surgeons then aspirate the loosened fat through small cannulas, usually 1 to 3 millimetres wide, through small skin openings.[1] Variants layer additional energy on top of the tumescent base: ultrasound-assisted, power-assisted, laser-assisted, radiofrequency-assisted and water-jet-assisted liposuction, the last often used in lipedema.[1][14] Abdominal etching is a high-definition style that accentuates muscle contours.[1]

The lidocaine in the solution is metabolised mainly in the liver by the CYP3A4 enzyme, with an elimination half-life of about 90 to 120 minutes, and drugs that inhibit that enzyme can raise lidocaine levels.[23] Epinephrine is commonly paired with lidocaine to prolong the local effect and reduce bleeding.[23]

The American Society of Plastic Surgeons lists the abdomen, hips, thighs and buttocks as typical liposuction areas, and also the chest, back, face, neck, upper arms, inner knees and calves; it can be combined with procedures such as facelifts, breast reduction or tummy tuck.[24] The society says candidates are generally people of normal weight with localised fat, that firm, elastic skin reshapes better than loose skin from stretch marks, weight loss or aging, and that liposuction is not effective for cellulite.[24]

Tumescent infiltration is used because it allows fat to be removed with the patient awake, without the sedatives or narcotics that other approaches rely on.[1][21] Surgeons use this fine control for abdominal etching and other high-definition styles that accentuate muscle outlines, which is the look most associated with appearance-focused body contouring.[1]

Early fat-removal surgery in the 1920s, associated with French surgeon Charles Dujarier, was set back by a 1926 complication, and cannula suction took shape in Rome in the mid-1970s with Arpad and Giorgio Fischer, whose 1977 review covered 245 cases.[1] Yves-Gerard Illouz extended suction to the whole body and developed a wet technique with injected fluid.[1]

In the 1980s American dermatologists, led by Jeffrey Klein, published the tumescent approach using large volumes of very dilute lidocaine and epinephrine so surgery could be done under local anesthesia; Wikipedia credits Klein and Patrick Lillis as its inventors and dates its marketing to the 1990s.[1][21] It reached Australia in the early 1990s, where Daniel Lanzer is named among the first to use it.[21]

The technique spread through dermatology and plastic surgery in the 1990s, and the first national safety survey of tumescent liposuction, covering 15,336 patients, was published in 1995.[3] By 2015, liposuction had overtaken breast augmentation as the most common cosmetic procedure in the United States, according to Wikipedia.[1]

Fat cells that are removed are permanently gone, but studies cited by Wikipedia report that total body fat generally returns to its earlier level within a few months, with some redistribution to untreated areas such as the abdomen, if lifestyle is unchanged.[1] The same source describes liposuction as a contouring tool, not a weight-loss method.[1]

A 2023 letter in Archives of Dermatological Research examined the metabolic effects of tumescent liposuction.[15] A 2018 review of liposuction evidence compared suction-assisted with ultrasound- and laser-assisted techniques.[14] A 2013 review in Clinics in Plastic Surgery covers the tumescent technique itself.[16]

In a 2011 study cited by Wikipedia, overall body fat returned to close to pre-treatment levels within a few months even when diet and exercise were maintained, with most of the regained fat in the abdomen, and the difference in visceral fat between groups was not significant.[21] The American Society of Plastic Surgeons states liposuction is not a substitute for diet and exercise.[24]

A 1999 New England Journal of Medicine report identified five deaths after tumescent liposuction and noted that, because adverse-event reporting is not mandatory, the true incidence of complications and deaths is unknown; it also observed that recommended lidocaine doses are as high as 55 mg/kg while safety data are scarce.[4]

A 1995 survey of dermatologic surgeons covered 15,336 patients, and a 2002 survey examined office-based tumescent liposuction safety.[3][5] A 2016 analysis estimated maximal safe tumescent lidocaine dosages.[7] Wikipedia states that lidocaine toxicity has been linked to deaths in liposuction and that overall mortality is reported at roughly one per 10,000 cases as of 2011.[1]

Other reported complications are bleeding, infection, blood clots, organ perforation, seroma, numbness, skin irregularities and dimpling.[1] Wikipedia also cites a 2015 study of 4,534 patients treated by board-certified plastic surgeons in which 1.5 percent had complications, with higher risk at larger volumes, and CDC reports of deaths among US patients who had cosmetic surgery abroad, mostly from embolism.[1] Training requirements vary by US state, according to Wikipedia.[1]

Wikipedia's tumescent liposuction article cites a 2011 review by Tierney and colleagues that judged the technique safe, while noting that deaths were reported during its first decade of use and that European literature had recorded 23 deaths over five years by 2002; the main lethal complications described were bacterial infection such as necrotizing fasciitis, hemorrhage, abdominal perforation and pulmonary embolism.[21] The same article notes that many US states do not require physicians performing the procedure to have specific training.[21]

Lidocaine itself is described as having a standard maximum safe dose far lower than the figures cited for tumescent solutions in the 1999 NEJM report. Overdose, from excessive dosing or prolonged infiltration, can cause central nervous system effects first, then cardiovascular effects, and lipid emulsion therapy is increasingly used to reverse it.[23][4][7]

Lipedema is a condition of painful, symmetrical fat accumulation, almost exclusively in women; Wikipedia gives an estimate that it affects about 11 percent of women, with reported figures ranging widely, and notes it is often misdiagnosed or underdiagnosed.[22] A 2012 study reported good long-term results of tumescent liposuction in lipedema, and Dutch guidelines on lipedema were published in 2017.[8][9] Wikipedia states that the highest-quality studies involve tumescent local anesthesia, describes follow-ups at about 4 and 8 years, and cites a 2020 international consensus conference on using it to prevent progression; it also notes that surgery can damage lymphatic vessels, that treatment is not a cure and may need several procedures, and that some US insurers began covering it as medically necessary in 2020.[22]
Tumescent harvesting is also used to collect adipose tissue for stem-cell and fat-grafting work, and a 2006 study found that harvesting method influenced stem cell yield.[10]

Human data include large surveys of safety, a lipedema outcome study, and pharmacologic studies of lidocaine dosing.[3][5][7][8] The 1995 survey sent questionnaires to 1,778 members of the American Society for Dermatologic Surgery,[3] and the 2002 survey asked about office-based tumescent liposuction safety.[5]

A randomized trial examined efficacy of a lower lidocaine concentration in the tumescent solution,[17] and earlier side-to-side trials compared tumescent liposuction with ultrasound-assisted tumescent liposuction and with external ultrasound afterward.[18][19] Lidocaine and epinephrine blood levels during tumescent liposuction were measured in a 1996 study.[20]

Registered trials include a lidocaine maximum-safe-dose study (NCT00977028), a trial of cold versus warm tumescent solution in arm liposculpture (NCT06865911) with 52 participants, and a trial of tranexamic acid in tumescent solution (NCT06648265) with 78 participants.[11][12][13]

Reviews of technique variants include a 2018 Annals of Plastic Surgery review that screened 9,972 articles and identified 25 comparing standard suction-assisted liposuction with ultrasound- or laser-assisted methods.[14]

Variants layer energy devices on top of the tumescent base: ultrasound-assisted, power-assisted, laser-assisted, radiofrequency-assisted and water-jet-assisted liposuction.[1][14] Water-assisted liposuction, developed by Ziah Taufig and used in lipedema, is lymph-sparing, usually done under general anesthesia, and technically not considered tumescent.[22] Fat removed by liposuction is the source tissue for fat grafting procedures that move fat to other areas, and for stem cell research.[10]

Non-surgical fat-reduction approaches and abdominoplasty address overlapping goals; the American Society of Plastic Surgeons notes that extra skin after liposuction may require additional surgery to remove and tighten it.[24]

lore.intro: Public discussion of liposuction centres on what it can and cannot change about body shape and whether local-anesthesia versions are safer. The claims below are drawn from how surgeons' societies and reference works describe the procedure.

claims.claim: Fat cells removed by liposuction are gone for good.
claims.believers: Patients and surgeons describe removed fat cells as not growing back in the treated spot.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes removal is permanent locally, but studies cited there report overall body fat returning within months if lifestyle is unchanged, with redistribution to untreated areas.[1][21]

claims.claim: Liposuction is a way to lose weight.
claims.believers: Some people consider it as a route to weight loss.
claims.experts: The American Society of Plastic Surgeons says it is not a treatment for obesity or substitute for diet and exercise, and Wikipedia describes it as a contouring tool.[1][24]

claims.claim: Tumescent local anesthesia is safer than general anesthesia.
claims.believers: Dermatologic surgeons who developed the method describe avoiding sedatives and narcotics as a benefit.[1][21]
claims.experts: A 2011 review judged the technique safe, but a 1999 NEJM report documented deaths and noted that reporting is not mandatory, so incidence is unknown.[4][21]

claims.claim: It can sculpt visible abs and muscle definition.
claims.believers: Cosmetic surgeons offer high-definition liposuction and abdominal etching to accentuate muscle outlines.[1]
claims.experts: Evidence for this is mostly surgeon-reported outcomes; systematic comparison has focused on energy-assisted versus suction-assisted techniques.[14]

claims.claim: Lipedema fat can be treated with tumescent liposuction.
claims.believers: Patients and surgeons report symptom relief and shape improvement.[8]
claims.experts: A 2012 study reports good long-term results, and a 2020 consensus conference addressed its use, though surgery can damage lymphatic vessels and may need repeat procedures.[8][22]

claims.claim: Cheaper overseas liposuction is a bargain.
claims.believers: Surgery abroad is sometimes sought as a lower-cost option.
claims.experts: Wikipedia cites CDC reports of deaths among US patients who had cosmetic surgery abroad, mostly from embolism, and notes training requirements vary.[1]

card.summary: Liposuction under local anesthesia using large volumes of dilute lidocaine; the standard technique, with safety data from large surgeon surveys.
card.note: Lidocaine toxicity is the technique-specific concern reported in the literature.

quick.overview:
Tumescent liposuction fills fat with dilute numbing solution before suction, so patients can stay awake under local anesthesia. It was developed by dermatologists in the 1980s and is now a standard technique.

Large surveys of dermatologic surgeons have examined its safety, and studies report good long-term results in lipedema.
quick.mechanism: Lidocaine numbs the tissue and epinephrine narrows blood vessels, reducing bleeding and bruising while fat is aspirated through thin cannulas.
quick.risks: The literature reports lidocaine toxicity as a concern, plus general liposuction risks such as infection, bleeding, clots and contour irregularity. A 1999 report noted deaths and that reporting is not mandatory, so incidence is uncertain.

chain: Dilute anesthetic swells and numbs fat
Thin cannulas remove fat cells from chosen areas
angle.text: Tumescent liposuction removes fat cells from specific areas, changing the shape of the abdomen, flanks, thighs, arms or neck. The local-anesthetic approach lets patients avoid general anesthesia, and the fat cells that are removed do not grow back in that spot.
